edges.description: Elevated intradiscal pressure forces nucleus pulposus fibrocartilage into perivertebral venous or arterial channels.
Acute intervertebral disc disruption and raised intradiscal pressure elicit sudden axial back or neck pain at onset.
Intraluminal fibrocartilaginous emboli occlude spinal arterial perfusion and cause downstream parenchymal infarction.
Cytotoxic edema and parenchymal necrosis produce characteristic T2-hyperintense and DWI-restricted intrinsic spinal cord lesions.
Infarction of anterior horn motor neurons and long white-matter tracts causes abrupt sensorimotor and autonomic myelopathy.
Abrupt loss of spinal cord tract conduction manifests clinically as acute non-inflammatory myelopathy.
Bilateral corticospinal and anterior horn infarction at thoracic or lumbar levels causes paraplegia.
Incomplete thoracolumbar corticospinal/anterior horn ischemia causes lower-limb weakness (paraparesis).
Cervical spinal cord infarction produces four-limb paralysis (quadriplegia/tetraplegia).
Spinothalamic and dorsal tract ischemia produces bilateral sensory loss with a spinal sensory level.
Anterolateral spinothalamic tract infarction selectively impairs pain and temperature sensation below the lesion.
Acute anterior horn and spinal shock produce absent tendon reflexes and flaccid tone at presentation.
Lateral horn and descending autonomic tract injury causes neurogenic bladder and urinary incontinence.
Disruption of spinal autonomic pathways causes loss of anal sphincter control and fecal incontinence.
Axial vertebral compression combined with Valsalva raises intradiscal pressure and drives nucleus pulposus extrusion.
